issues.legal_issue: An interlocutory mandatory injunction is unwarranted when it creates a new state of affairs instead of restoring the last uncontested status quo and the circumstances do not justify that exceptional relief.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought contractual relief against a developer and a contractor, and an interim consent order barred the defendants from dealing with specified flats and parking spaces.
While the suit remained pending, the court ordered the contractor to hand over additional flats and parking spaces to the plaintiff.
The contractor had possession of the additional flats, and the order requiring their handover did not restore a status quo that the contractor had altered.
The contractor’s contractual dispute with the developer was pending in arbitration.
issues.conclusion: The interlocutory mandatory injunction exceeded the High Court’s jurisdiction and was set aside; the earlier interim restraint against dealing with the specified flats and parking spaces was restored until disposal of the suit or further modification.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XXXIX of the Code of Civil Procedure, an interlocutory mandatory injunction is an exceptional equitable remedy. Under Dorab Cawasji Warden v. Coomi Sorab Warden, the applicant must show a strong case for trial, a need to prevent irreparable or serious injury, and a balance of convenience in the applicant’s favour. Such relief generally preserves or restores the last uncontested status quo, or undoes an act done illegally; it is not ordinarily used to establish a new state of affairs. The Court followed Metro Marins v. Bonus Watch Co., Kishore Kumar Khaitan v. Praveen Kumar Singh, and Purshottam Vishandas Raheja v. Shrichand Vishandas Raheja.

predicates.appeal_from_interlocutory_mandatory_inju: The proceeding is an appeal from an order granting mandatory relief before the final determination of the suit.
predicates.order_changes_possession_or_control: The order requires a party to transfer possession or control rather than merely preserve existing arrangements.
predicates.clear_status_quo_alteration_by_target_pa: The party against whom relief is sought clearly altered the last uncontested state of affairs.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns an interim mandatory order that changes possession or control and the target party did not clearly alter the prior status quo, the order is unwarranted.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot use the principle of moulding relief at an interlocutory stage to grant relief that should be considered when finally deciding the suit.
material_facts: While the plaintiff’s suit and interim application were pending, the plaintiff and the developer entered into settlement terms providing for additional flats and parking spaces to be handed over to the plaintiff.
The courts below relied on the changed circumstances created by those terms to order the contractor to hand over the additional property before the suit was decided.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred by relying on moulding of relief to grant mandatory relief at the interlocutory stage; that principle could be applied when considering final relief in the suit.
issues.legal_principle: Gaiv Dinshaw Irani v. Tehmtan Irani concerned moulding relief while finally disposing of proceedings to do substantial justice. It did not authorize granting such relief at an interlocutory stage. The Court distinguished that decision on this basis.

predicates.interlocutory_relief_proceeding: The court is deciding an application for relief while the main suit remains pending.
predicates.final_suit_rights_undecided: The parties’ substantive rights in the suit have not yet been finally determined.
predicates.court_uses_changed_circumstances_to_gran: The court relies on circumstances that arose during the case to order relief that substantially resolves the claim before trial.

issues.definition: If substantive rights remain undecided in an interlocutory proceeding, changed circumstances cannot be used to grant relief that is in substance final.

issues.legal_issue: A settlement between contracting parties cannot be used to impose a new contractual obligation on a person who was not a party to that settlement.
material_facts: The plaintiff and the developer entered into settlement terms requiring the developer to provide additional flats and parking spaces to the plaintiff.
The contractor was not a party to those settlement terms, although it had a separate development agreement with the developer and was a party to a tripartite agreement.
The order directed the contractor to hand over property to satisfy the developer’s settlement obligation to the plaintiff.
issues.conclusion: The settlement terms between the plaintiff and the developer could not bind the contractor or justify directing it to discharge the developer’s obligation; the contractor remained bound by the agreements to which it was a party.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that an agreement between parties inter partes cannot be thrust upon a nonparty. It held that the contractor could be bound by its own development agreement and, at most, the tripartite agreement, but not by the separate settlement between the other parties.

predicates.appeal_from_interlocutory_order: The proceeding is an appeal from an order made before the final determination of the underlying suit.
predicates.settlement_excludes_party_targeted_by_or: The person targeted by the order did not enter into the settlement on which the order relies.
predicates.order_enforces_settlement_obligation_aga: The order requires the excluded person to perform an obligation created by the settlement.

issues.definition: When an interlocutory order enforces a settlement obligation against someone who did not join that settlement, the settlement cannot bind that person.
